title: Feelings in depth
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: KOREAN WILL NOT LET YOU STATE ANOTHER PERSON'S INNER STATE DIRECTLY. Jeo-neun gippeoyo is right, and Chingu-neun gippeoyo is not. A feeling that is somebody else's is said with the ACTION shape gippeohaeyo — you can see what a person does, and you cannot see what they feel.

THE SHAPE IS THE DESCRIPTIVE VERB PLUS haeyo, AND IT IS ALREADY IN THE COURSE. gippeo + haeyo, seulpeo + haeyo — the same -a/-eo stem the ladder has been conjugating since L1-M4, with haeyo on the end. L1-M1's joahaeyo IS this rule already frozen: joayo is it-is-good-to-me, joahaeyo is likes it.

It is written as ONE token, not two. joahaeyo has been one word since L1-M1, and gippeohaeyo, seulpeohaeyo follow it. A hyphen in this course means a particle boundary and nothing else, and a space would make the index read haeyo as a separate verb.

NUANCE HERE IS DEGREE, NOT NEW WORDS. neomu (too much of it, and in speech simply very), jom and jogeum (a bit), L3-M1's byeollo and geoui with their obligatory negative, and L2-M1's gwaenchanayo for the honest middle. The word in front of the feeling is what moves it.

-gess- IS CONJECTURE, NOT A SECOND FUTURE. himdeulgesseoyo is that must be hard, masitgesseoyo is that looks good, algesseoyo is I see, I have got it. It is what Korean says to sympathise, which is why it lives with the feelings. Every plan is still L1-M6's -l geoyeyo, and no second future is opened here.
EVERY CLAUSE IN THIS MODULE IS PRESENT. A feeling in the past — how the day felt, how the exam went — is L3-M10's business, and the -eoss- past is not written on a feeling verb anywhere in this file.

REGISTER: this module stays neutral, and that is a decision rather than an oversight. Feelings are what friends talk about, and the forms that would earn an informal chip are banmal, which L1 banned and L3 does not lift. Warmth is carried by -gess- to sympathise and jom to soften instead.

words.note: Its dictionary sense is too much, but in ordinary speech it is simply very: neomu joayo is I love it, not I like it excessively.
A descriptive verb, so it is a whole sentence on its own and needs no am. It may only describe the speaker; for anyone else see gippeohaeyo.

sentences.trap: neomu is not a warning. An English speaker reads too and hears a complaint, but neomu gippeoyo is unmixed good news; the complaint reading needs a bad thing after it, as in neomu bissayo.
sentences.sound: JEO-neun NEO-mu GI-ppeo-yo. The pp in gippeoyo is tense and unaspirated — no puff of air, closer to a hard English b than to p.

variations.changed: jogeum for neomu — the same sentence with the degree turned down
L3-M1's jeongmal, which asserts the feeling is true rather than large

mistake.why: gippeoyo is already the whole predicate. There is no am to add, and isseoyo is a different verb: Jeo-neun neomu gippeoyo.

sentences.usage: Good news you have just been given, and the first thing you say back.

words.note: gippeo + haeyo: the feeling turned into something a person is seen doing. It is the only shape available once the feeling is not the speaker's.

sentences.trap: THE FRIEND TAKES -ga, NOT -neun. A topic is what the whole sentence is about, and here the sentence is about what the friend is visibly doing, so the plain subject particle is what it wants.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu-ga GI-ppeo-hae-yo. Said at speed the eo and hae run together, but the word is never shortened in writing.

variations.changed: L1-M7's dongsaeng, with -i because the name ends in a consonant

variations.cue: My friend is over the moon.
variations.changed: the degree word sits in front of the action shape unchanged

mistake.why: gippeoyo can only be said of yourself. Somebody else's gladness is Chingu-ga gippeohaeyo.

sentences.usage: Reporting how another person is, when you can see it on them.
sentences.mnemonic: Mine is felt, theirs is done.

words.note: The same pair as gippeoyo: seulpeoyo of yourself, seulpeohaeyo of anybody else. The second form is the one a learner never guesses.

sentences.trap: jogeum and L2-M1's jom are the same word, and jom is the softer of the two — jogeum measures the sadness, jom apologises for mentioning it.
sentences.sound: JEO-neun JO-geum SEUL-peo-yo. seul is one syllable; the eu is the flat unrounded vowel, not English 'ul'.

variations.changed: the same feeling moved onto somebody else, so the action shape takes over
L3-M1's byeollo, which still cannot stand without its negative

mistake.why: Twice wrong in one short sentence: the feeling of another person needs seulpeohaeyo, and the subject wants -ga. Chingu-ga seulpeohaeyo.

sentences.usage: Admitting to a small sadness without making it the whole conversation.

words.note: The mood you are in on a given day, not your character. It is the SUBJECT of the sentence, so it takes -i and the feeling word describes it.

sentences.trap: There is no you anywhere in this question. Korean leaves the listener out once the situation has named them, and adding one would make the question pointed rather than kind.
sentences.sound: O-neul GI-bu-ni EO-ttae-yo. gibun-i runs together as GI-bu-ni — the particle takes the noun's last consonant with it.

variations.cue: I'm in a good mood today.
variations.changed: L1-M9's joayo answering the question it was made for
L2-M1's gwaenchanayo as the honest middle answer

mistake.why: -eun would set the mood up against something else you had in mind. The plain question is Oneul gibun-i eottaeyo?

sentences.usage: Asking after somebody at the start of a day, or the morning after bad news.

sentences.cue: I'm in a bad mood right now.

words.note: The opposite of joayo. On a mood it says out of sorts or cross, which is a smaller claim than English a bad mood usually makes.

sentences.trap: TWO SUBJECT-LIKE PHRASES, AND BOTH ARE CORRECT. jeo-neun sets the topic and gibun-i is the grammatical subject; the sentence is as-for-me, the-mood-is-bad. English has no room for both, so a learner drops one and says the wrong thing.
sentences.sound: JEO-neun JI-geum GI-bu-ni NA-ppa-yo. The pp is tense: hold the lips and release without a puff.

variations.cue: I'm not in a great mood.
variations.changed: the same news said gently, with byeollo and its negative

variations.cue: I'm in a bad mood today.
variations.changed: the topic dropped altogether once the conversation knows who

mistake.why: The particle is what marks gibun as the thing being described. Written out it is Jeo-neun jigeum gibun-i nappayo.

sentences.usage: Warning somebody, kindly, that this is not the moment.

words.note: Excitement that is already happening, not anticipation of something later. A trip you are on is sinnayo; a trip next month is not.

sentences.trap: English excited points forward — I'm excited for Friday. sinnayo points at now, so the Friday version is a plan sentence with L1-M6's -l geoyeyo in it, not this word.
sentences.sound: JEO-neun JEONG-mal SIN-na-yo. The n doubles across the seam and is held: sin-NA, not si-na.

variations.changed: byeollo with an, the negative it cannot do without
neomu raising the degree instead of jeongmal asserting it

mistake.why: The stem ends in -na and takes -yo directly. It is sinnayo.

sentences.usage: The moment something you were waiting for actually starts.

words.note: The thing feared is the SUBJECT and does the frightening, so the exam takes -i. There is no of anywhere in the Korean sentence.
Unease with no single object — the feeling before results come out. Its -haeyo is part of the word itself, not the rule that builds gippeohaeyo.

sentences.trap: museoweoyo IS ALREADY BACKWARDS. Korean says the exam is frightening and lets jeo-neun say who to; an English speaker reaches for a word meaning I fear and marks the exam as an object, which is not a sentence here.
sentences.sound: JEO-neun SI-heo-mi MU-seo-weo-yo. siheom-i is SI-heo-mi, and the weo is one glide, close to English 'wuh'.

variations.changed: the unfocused feeling, which needs no thing to fear at all
the topic dropped, leaving the frightening thing on its own

mistake.why: Nothing is being done to the exam, so -eul has no work here: Jeo-neun siheom-i museoweoyo.

sentences.usage: Saying what is weighing on you, to a friend or to a teacher.
sentences.mnemonic: The scary thing is the subject.

sentences.cue: The class is a bit tough.

words.note: Hard as in draining, said of work, a class or a week. Difficult-to-understand is a different word, and this one is about the toll rather than the puzzle.

sentences.trap: jom is doing politeness here, not measurement. Dropping it leaves Sueop-i himdeureoyo, which is a complaint; with jom it is an admission.
sentences.sound: SU-eo-bi JOM HIM-deu-reo-yo. sueop-i is SU-eo-bi — the p softens to b between vowels.

variations.cue: Working is a bit hard going.
variations.changed: L3-M2's modifier in front of geo, so the hard thing is an activity
jeongmal in place of jom, and the admission becomes a complaint

mistake.why: -eun sets the class against your other classes. To say only that it is tough, use Sueop-i jom himdeureoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling a classmate or a teacher how it is going, without asking for anything.

words.note: himdeureoyo with -gess- inside it. The ending guesses at what you cannot know first-hand, which is why it is the polite way to answer somebody else's bad news.

sentences.trap: -gess- IS NOT A FUTURE, whatever half the material a learner meets will say. himdeulgesseoyo is about right now and about somebody else; every plan in this course is still L1-M6's -l geoyeyo.
sentences.sound: GEU-geo-neun JEONG-mal HIM-deul-GE-sseo-yo. The ss is tense — hold it and release sharply.

variations.changed: the same ending on to know, where it softens I know into I see
-gess- guessing from the look of a thing rather than from what you were told

mistake.why: Without -gess- you are claiming to know how their week felt. Guessing is Geugeo-neun jeongmal himdeulgesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Answering somebody who has just told you something hard.

words.note: Not the organ but the inner self — where a decision, a kindness or a hurt sits. gibun is today's weather; maeum is the climate.

sentences.trap: maeum-i apayo is not a medical sentence. L2-M8's apayo does bodies and this does grief, and the difference is carried entirely by which noun takes -i.
sentences.sound: JEO-neun MA-eu-mi A-pa-yo. maeum is two syllables, ma-eum, never one.

variations.changed: the topic dropped, and neomu on a hurt rather than on a gladness

variations.cue: My friend is sad. It hurts to see.
variations.changed: the two halves of the module in one turn — their feeling, then yours

mistake.why: Nothing is done to the heart; it is what hurts. Jeo-neun maeum-i apayo.

sentences.usage: What you say when somebody else's news has landed on you.
sentences.mnemonic: gibun is the day, maeum is the person.

comprehensionPool.cue: I'm not in a great mood.
The class is a bit tough.
